source.title: Behemoth: Benchmarking Unlearning in LLMs Using Fully Synthetic Data

page_placements.theme: Non-propagation to related, implied or multi-hop facts; target inferable from retained knowledge

record.tranche_reason: In a synthetic setting, the study fine-tunes a model to remap one relationship and tests whether a perfectly correlated relationship is also remapped. It reports that the original correlated information can remain accessible, and explicitly interprets this as an output change without removal of the information.
record.gate_note: The paper's activation-patching results are diagnostic measurements, not tests of post-unlearning recovery. Results cited from other studies are excluded. Plots show additional rank-specific outcomes, but the text does not state their individual numerical values.
record.test_reason: In a fully synthetic 31M model, fine-tuning to 'forget' relationship r1 leaves a perfectly correlated r2 intact. The authors read this as an output edit without removing the information. That bears on version C's 'blocks access rather than deleting' clause, in a new setting with no LLM unlearning method. T3 fits better than T5 because the result agrees with C rather than arguing a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that even with perfectly dependent facts, fine-tuning to forget r1 can leave r2 intact, which they read as editing outputs without removing information. They add that this depends heavily, and unexpectedly, on fine-tuning hyperparameters such as rank and layer choice. They caution that the synthetic grammar is not representative of natural language.
record.recipe_differences: Uses full-rank or LoRA fine-tuning to remap synthetic tabular facts in a model trained from scratch; it does not apply the cited LLM unlearning methods or recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Forgetting of the correlated relationship varies with fine-tuning rank; the dependent-relationship result decreases as rank increases.

fits_no_version.finding: In the nested dataset, forgetting r1 has no effect on the implied relationship r̂1; dependent editing success is practically 0 in all cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-based forgetting does not propagate to implied or multi-hop facts (deep unlearning / ripple effects).

fits_no_version.finding: ROME single edits of r1 succeed 100% but update the correlated r2 only 90% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fact edits do not fully propagate to logically equivalent facts.

record.problems: The relevant evidence comes from a small, fully synthetic 31-million-parameter model and perfectly correlated binary relationships; the authors state that the grammar and data structure are not representative of natural-language data. The relevant text gives qualitative results rather than per-rank numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Other editing tasks and rank-specific plot points were not recorded because they do not test a recovery version or their individual values are not stated in the text. Activation-patching and rank-estimation measurements do not test post-unlearning recovery.

untested.parts: No standard unlearning method, chance-level targeting, or attack evaluation. Forgetting r1 does cut remaining accuracy to 70–80% (simple dataset), but this is a cost of remap fine-tuning, not of a claimed unlearning method.
No activation-direction ablation; only indirect evidence of retained information via a correlated fact.
No prompt-based attacks. Querying the correlated r2 is a structural probe, not a prompting attack.

missing.what: LoRA layer-choice result: forgetting r1 either mostly forgets r2 or almost entirely preserves it, depending on layers (first-block attention or last-block MLP).
Full-FT layer-subset dependent remapping success for forgetting r1, roughly 0.5–0.85.
Forgetting r1 drops remaining accuracy to 70–80% (simple dataset), a general-ability cost of remap fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: Weak fit to the phenomenon. Toy 31M model trained from scratch, with 'forgetting' defined as remapping to one value. No real LLM unlearning methods and no recovery attacks. Evidence is qualitative in the text, with numbers only in plots. The link to C rests on the authors' interpretation, not on an internal-edit attack. None of the study's authors are among the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test a method that brings targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance while preserving general ability and then evaluates simple recovery attacks.
Fine-tuning is used to remap facts, not as a post-unlearning recovery attack using a small relearning set.

No activation direction is ablated. The study tests retained access through a perfectly correlated relationship in a synthetic model, not the other internal-edit mechanisms or real LLM unlearning methods.
No quantization recovery attack is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No newer counter-method is evaluated for resistance to recovery attacks.

rows.subject: Pythia-31m Transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained from random initialization on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on r1 tuples to remap all objects for relationship r1 to one value; tested whether the correlated r2 tuple was also remapped.

conditions.value: perfectly correlated r1 and r2; both binary
forget r1 by remapping all its objects to one value

rows.measure: Remapping success on the fully dependent r2 tuple
rows.note: The paper says the r2 forgetting attempt is almost completely ineffective with full fine-tuning, although the training data for this forgetting task contains r1 tuples and not r2 tuples. The authors interpret this as evidence that the output changed without removing the original information.
rows.check: Linking to C is defensible only through C's 'blocks rather than deletes' clause; no direction is ablated. The measure is dependent (r2) remapping success, not recovery of r1 itself. Baseline: r2 accuracy before editing is not stated. Appendix Fig. 26 shows layer-subset full-FT dependent success of roughly 0.5–0.85, which sits uneasily with 'almost completely ineffective'; that figure may cover layer subsets rather than the all-layer run.

relation.reason: Its own results on r2 retention after r1 forgetting bear on version C, though indirectly.

tranche.reason: New synthetic from-scratch setting with a result on C's blocks-rather-than-deletes clause. No LLM unlearning methods or recovery attacks are used.

source_check.notes: The link to C is indirect: no activation direction is ablated and no r1 recovery is measured. 'Forgetting' means remapping all r1 objects to one value by fine-tuning. The model is a from-scratch 31M Pythia-architecture model on a toy grammar, which the authors say does not represent natural language.

statements.correction: Text: with full finetuning, 'forgetting' of the fully dependent r2 tuple is 'almost completely ineffective'. The forgetting set has only r1 tuples. Model is a Pythia-31m architecture trained from scratch on synthetic data.
Text: r2 forgetting decreases with finetuning rank (Section 4.9). With LoRA, forgetting r1 gives either mostly forgetting r2 or almost entirely preserving it, depending on layer choice (Section 5.2).

Nested (Section 4.10): forgetting r1 has no effect on forgetting r-hat1, and dependent editing success is practically 0 in all cases. Correlated (Section 4.9): a ROME single-tuple r1 remap worked 100% of the time, but the dependent r2 updated only 90%.
statements.problem: The ROME 100%/90% figures come from the correlated dataset (Section 4.9), but the statement lists them under 'Nested dataset'. The nested section gives no ROME dependent figure in the text.
